Takasaki Daruma is a regional craft centered historically in the Toyooka area of Takasaki, Gunma. Takasaki City says it was called Toyooka Daruma for roughly 140 years before Toyooka Village merged into Takasaki City in 1955. The city's page also notes the crane-and-turtle face motifs and later traditional-craft and trademark recognition.
Takasaki City says Daruma making in the area is traditionally attributed to Yamagata Tomogoro of Toyooka Village a little over two centuries ago.
Takasaki City explains that early Daruma production was seasonal, taking place after the rice harvest and wheat sowing, from autumn into the following spring.
Takasaki City connects the expansion of local Daruma production after the 1859 opening of Yokohama port with improved access to imported scarlet red pigment.
Takasaki City says the number of local Daruma-making households/workshops had grown to about 18 around 1909 and states that 72 craftspeople currently carry on the tradition on the cited city page.

Takasaki City describes a historical connection between red Daruma and protection against smallpox: red was believed to repel harmful forces, and red Daruma could be placed near children during outbreaks.

Takasaki City reports that an 1829 source called Takasaki Danzu-sho preserves text and an image of Daruma being sold at a market in Tamachi, providing evidence for an early urban Daruma-market tradition.

Takasaki City has planned a Takasaki Daruma museum around four concepts: communicating the tradition, learning, passing skills on, and connecting people; proposed functions include exhibitions, making experiences, and presentation of manufacturing processes.
Takasaki City states that Takasaki Daruma was designated a Gunma Prefecture Furusato Traditional Craft in 1993.

Takasaki Daruma received a Japanese regional collective trademark. The Japan Patent Office lists registration number 5003697 and the Gunma Prefecture Daruma Manufacturers Cooperative Association as the rights holder for Daruma produced in Takasaki and the surrounding area.
Shorinzan Daruma-ji's official FAQ says that when facing the Daruma, the eye on the viewer's right is filled first. This corresponds to the Daruma's left eye.

Shorinzan Daruma-ji's official FAQ explicitly says that different Daruma colors do not inherently have different meanings in its own religious practice; the meaning comes from the wish placed into the Daruma and the eye-opening practice.
Shorinzan Daruma-ji explains the red body through Bodhidharma's red robe and the visual form of a seated monk wrapped in that robe.

Shorinzan Daruma-ji's official FAQ rejects the idea that Bodhidharma literally had no arms or legs; it says the rounded Daruma form represents him seated in meditation with his limbs hidden under the robe.

Shorinzan Daruma-ji advises placing its Daruma on the viewer's left side of a household kamidana if one is present, or otherwise in a place above eye level where the Daruma can symbolically watch over people.

The temple describes Daruma kaigen as an eye-opening prayer in which a priest places the first mark, after which the owner may enlarge the eye while making a wish. The second eye is completed after a safe year or the fulfillment of the wish.
Kofu City presents Koshu Daruma as a craft with a tradition of more than 400 years and says one origin tradition attributes the papier-mache technique to a monk who came from Kyoto.
Koshu Daruma was also called Yokozawa Daruma because it was historically made in the Yokozawa area of Kofu.
Kofu City says Koshu Daruma has been sold as a good-luck and misfortune-avoiding object at events including the Daijingu Setsubun festival and the Yumura Yakuyoke Jizoson festival.

Kofu City notes that before World War II many Koshu Daruma were sold with eyes already painted. Their pupils are placed low so that a Daruma displayed high on a household shelf appears to look toward the worshipper; this led to the name 'shitami daruma,' or downward-looking Daruma.
Kofu City describes Koshu Daruma as having a deeply modeled face, high nose, horizontally elongated oval eyes, and crane/turtle forms in the brows and facial hair.
Kofu City says roughly ten production processes are performed by hand in the traditional craft.
Kofu City presents the association with warlord Takeda Shingen as a theory or motif tradition rather than an uncontested historical fact.

Kofu City describes a parent-and-child Daruma tradition revived in 1967. The white cocoon-like form is linked with Yamanashi's former sericulture economy, wishes for good harvests, household safety, descendants, and hopes for children's advancement.
Saitama Prefecture says Koshigaya Daruma is traditionally said to have been started in the Kyoho era by a man called Darukichi, while noting that the story is not certain.
Saitama Prefecture says Koshigaya Daruma is made by pasting washi over a wooden mold, producing a light figure known for righting itself well.
Saitama Prefecture describes Koshigaya Daruma as having a high nose and a gentle, elegant face.
Saitama Prefecture notes that Koshigaya Hariko Daruma was designated a prefectural traditional handicraft in 1984.

Konosu Akamono is a Saitama folk-craft tradition of red-painted molded figures. Research published through J-STAGE notes that Daruma and lion heads are major modern products, while historically the repertoire included many other figures.
The Konosu Akamono study connects red-colored folk toys with beliefs about warding off smallpox and protecting children, placing Daruma within a wider historical family of red protective toys.
Konosu Akamono uses toso, a molded material made from paulownia sawdust mixed with paste. This differs from the papier-mache construction of many Takasaki or Koshigaya Daruma.
The Konosu study notes that toso figures were relatively light and durable compared with clay figures or more crushable papier-mache, which helped them travel over wider markets.
Shirakawa City preserves a set of 19 clay molds for Shirakawa Daruma, in large, medium, and small sizes; the set is a city-designated important cultural property.

Shirakawa City says the Daruma were originally sold as lucky objects at the first regular market of the lunar year, and that the market later became known as the Daruma Market as Daruma sales came to dominate it.
Shirakawa City states that its Daruma Market is held on February 11.

Shirakawa City says the local Daruma tradition is associated with domain lord Matsudaira Sadanobu and with artist Tani Buncho in the development/coloring tradition; the city also preserves an important Daruma painting connected to Sadanobu.
Sendai City describes Matsukawa Daruma, a representative Sendai papier-mache craft, as blue and as having its eyes already painted, contrasting it with the familiar red blank-eyed Daruma type.
Sendai City materials describe the Matsukawa Daruma tradition as being continued by specialist makers in Sendai and as part of the city's inherited craft culture.

Matsuyama City's cultural heritage plan records a local tradition that Hime Daruma began as a craft commemorating the pregnancy of Empress Jingu during a legendary visit to Dogo; the same source explicitly notes that the historicity of some early imperial-visit traditions is uncertain.
Miharu Town describes its Daruma Market as a New Year tradition continuing since roughly the middle Edo period, around 300 years.
Miharu Town says Miharu Daruma range from small examples around 5–6 centimeters to large examples approaching 1 meter.

Miharu Town and its history museum describe the figure as relatively tall for its width, with a flattened head, reddish/deeply modeled face, long brows, strong facial hair, and vivid bluish outlines. The eyes are already painted.
Miharu Daruma is also called Takashiba Daruma because it is made at Takashiba in the Koriyama area.

The Miharu history museum lists multiple local Daruma types or names, including Miharu Daruma, Kabocha Daruma, Honjin Daruma, and Sesshu Daruma, illustrating diversity even within one regional production area.

Koriyama City materials describe Takashiba Deko-yashiki as a settlement of craft workshops that has produced papier-mache figures since the Edo period. The word deko is connected with a term for wooden dolls/figures.

Fukushima Prefecture's traditional-craft materials list several Daruma-related or self-righting traditions in the prefecture, including Fukushima Daruma, Shirakawa Daruma, Miharu papier-mache, and Aizu okiagari-koboshi.
Fukushima City describes Fukushima Daruma as a local tradition with about 150 years of history and highlights its somewhat elongated form, forceful eyes, and textured handmade surface.

National Diet Library materials describe okiagari-koboshi as self-righting figures associated with the spirit of 'seven times down, eight times up.' Daruma is one well-known form within a broader self-righting folk-toy world.

Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs Cultural Heritage Online database includes numerous works and objects titled or depicting Daruma, showing that the term appears across painting, folk material, crafts, and other museum collections.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes Hakuin Ekaku as an influential Zen monk and prolific painter who made many Bodhidharma portraits as teaching images. Its mid-eighteenth-century example is a hanging scroll in ink on paper.
The British Museum holds a papier-mache figure representing Daruma and describes Daruma as a popular image used in amulets, charms, and tumbler dolls connected with wishes.
The British Museum holds an Onna Daruma netsuke, a woman represented as Daruma, demonstrating historical transformation of the motif beyond the standard bearded male folk-doll form.
The British Museum holds a Daruma-shaped snowman netsuke. The ordinary Japanese word yukidaruma also means snowman, showing how the rounded Daruma silhouette entered everyday language and imagery.

Government of Japan material places Daruma within the wider history of Japanese dolls and says figures modeled on Bodhidharma's seated-meditation appearance began to be made in the eighteenth century.
Web Japan documents contemporary Daruma in new colors and designs and notes renewed interest in the object, while traditional craft and hand-painting continue.

Internet color charts for Daruma vary. This matters because Shorinzan Daruma-ji itself says colors do not carry fixed different meanings in its religious practice, while tourism and commercial guides may assign modern wish categories to colors.

A popular legend says Bodhidharma lost the use of his limbs after prolonged meditation, but Shorinzan Daruma-ji explicitly explains that its Daruma has arms and legs hidden by the robe. MuseBot should identify the limb-loss story as legend and give the temple explanation when discussing the modern doll's shape.

Red Daruma's association with disease protection is documented in local-history and folk-craft sources, especially in connection with historical smallpox beliefs. This is cultural history, not medical efficacy.

Modern Daruma use often turns the blank-eye custom into a goal-setting ritual: one eye marks commitment, the second marks completion. The object therefore functions both as a lucky object and as a visible reminder of unfinished effort.

Daruma can belong to temple practice, folk belief, craft, tourism, business, politics, art, souvenir culture, education, and personal goal-setting. The correct interpretation depends on the specific object's provenance and use.

No single Takasaki-style rule should be applied automatically to every Daruma. Matsukawa Daruma can be blue with painted eyes, Miharu Daruma have eyes from the start and a different body/face style, Koshu Daruma can have low-set eyes, and Koshigaya or Konosu traditions use different materials and techniques.
These records paraphrase source-backed Daruma information for many visitor types. Repetition is deliberate for retrieval robustness; it is not independent evidence.

When a visitor asks a Daruma question:

1. Identify whether they mean the generic Daruma concept or a specific regional/object form. 2. If the object has provenance, prioritize that provenance. 3. Give the shortest direct answer first. 4. Add regional/history detail only as needed. 5. Label legend as legend. 6. Label a temple's practice as that temple's practice. 7. Treat color meanings as variable unless the actual maker/museum gives a meaning. 8. Never claim a red Daruma prevents disease; explain the historical belief instead. 9. Never alter or handle a museum object to demonstrate the eye ritual or self-righting. 10. If asked an exact production statistic, give the source/date and note that numbers change. 11. If sources disagree, say so. 12. If the museum has not supplied object-specific maker/date/region data, do not invent it. 13. For children, use "falls down and gets back up" as the simplest resilience explanation. 14. For adult visitors, distinguish Bodhidharma, the folk doll, and the regional craft. 15. For specialists, include material, maker, date, provenance, inscriptions, eye state, region and source. 16. For religious questions, describe belief respectfully without claiming supernatural certainty. 17. For health questions, distinguish historical protective belief from medical reality. 18. For modern color questions, say that meanings vary and Shorinzan itself does not use a fixed color-code rule. 19. For eye questions, say the Shorinzan/Takasaki convention clearly and immediately mention that regional forms can differ. 20. When uncertain, say "I don't have enough information about this particular Daruma" rather than guessing.
